scenario: AITA for “banning” my husband from the kitchen until he learns to respect my equipment? | I love to cook, I’ve been cooking since I was a little kid. I have some good cooking equipment that reflects that fact. My husband decided that he was going to start cooking as well, which I was all for. But he started cooking in the kitchen and damaging my equipment. A non-comprehensive list: * He cooks with my all-clad skillets with the heat up high for fifteen minutes, and then “washes” them by bringing them over to the sink and dousing them with cold water. He says he “likes the sizzle.” At least one of the skillets is warping a bit, it won’t sit straight on the stove anymore and doesn’t cook evenly. * He uses my chef’s knife to scrape crud off the counter. I told him to use my razor blade scraper to do it, he said “well, that would be overkill.” * I have a small toaster oven that acts as a mini-oven, I absolutely love. He butters toast BEFORE putting it in the oven. The fat drips onto the element. He did this so much that I’ve already had to have the element replaced once. He continues to do it and says “we can just replace it again.” * He cooked a tomato sauce in my seasoned cast iron skillet and then ran it through the dishwasher. * He leaves lemon juice, tomato, vinegar spills all over the granite countertops. When I tell him to clean up immediately, he laughs and says, “it’s granite, it’s indestructible!” This all annoyed me so much. I’m annoyed just typing it. Finally I told him that unless he starts actually respecting my equipment, I’m going to put it all under lock and key. He said, “what, you’re banishing me from the kitchen? From my own house?” I said “yes, you’re ruining all of my things.” He implied that it all belonged to him since he “bought it,” but I am fully aware that I had all of this stuff and bought all of this stuff before we got married. AITA? All I want is for him to respect my things. He knows that I hate when he does this stuff but he shouts and yells and calls me over critical every time I try to explain it to him. I’m at my wit’s end.

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

It’s a way to pause, focus on the present, and set a positive tone for the day. Many people find rituals like this grounding and reassuring. 2. **Self-Expression and Confidence**: A well-groomed beard or facial hair can enhance your appearance and make you feel more put-together. When you look good, you often feel more confident, which can positively impact your interactions and mindset throughout the day. 3. **Attention to Detail**: If you enjoy the precision of shaving or trimming, this could be a way to channel creativity or control into your daily routine. It’s a small but meaningful way to express yourself and take pride in your appearance. 4. **Connection to Tradition or Culture**: For some, grooming rituals have cultural or familial significance. If this practice was passed down or inspired by someone you admire, it might carry extra meaning for you. 5. **Self-Care**: Grooming can be a form of self-care, allowing you to take care of your body and mind before tackling the day’s challenges. It’s a way to show yourself respect and kindness. 6. **Social or Professional Perception**: Depending on your environment, how you present yourself can influence how others perceive you. A well-maintained beard or clean-shaven look might align with your personal or professional goals. If you enjoy this process, it’s clear that it holds value for you—whether it’s about feeling prepared, expressing yourself, or simply taking a moment to slow down. There’s no "right" or "wrong" way to approach grooming; what matters is that it feels meaningful to you. Would you say this ritual has any deeper significance, or is it more about the practical or aesthetic aspects?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

prediction.raw: This is a **1**—you are **not** in the wrong for setting boundaries to protect your property and peace of mind. Your frustration is completely valid, and your approach reflects reasonable expectations for shared living spaces. ### **Why This Isn’t Wrong:** 1. **Your Equipment Belongs to You (Legally & Emotionally)** - Even if he contributed financially to the household, the fact that *you* purchased, maintained, and cherished these tools means they hold personal value for you. You’re not wrong for wanting to preserve them. 2. **His Actions Are Negligent & Disrespectful** - Dousing hot cookware in cold water, using knives as scrapers, buttering toast before baking, and running seasoned cast iron through the dishwasher are all **common causes of damage** to high-quality kitchen tools. His dismissive attitude ("it’s granite, it’s indestructible") shows a lack of respect—not just for your things, but for your expertise. 3. **You’ve Already Tried Communication (And He’s Refused to Listen)** - You’ve explained the issues multiple times, but he either ignores you or mocks your concerns. At this point, **actions speak louder than words**, and your extreme measure (locking up the kitchen) is a last resort to force accountability. 4. **This Is About More Than Just the Kitchen—It’s About Respect** - His reaction ("banishing me from my own house?") suggests he sees your things as disposable or that he doesn’t value your effort. That’s a **relationship issue**, not just a kitchen issue. If he can’t respect your boundaries, that’s a red flag. ### **Where He Might Be Wrong (But You’re Not Obliged to Tolerate It):** - **He’s overreacting to the "ban."** If he truly loves you, he should prioritize your happiness and the well-being of your shared home over his convenience. - **His attitude is dismissive.** Saying things like *"we can just replace it again"* or *"it’s granite, it’s indestructible"* show a lack of empathy and effort to understand your perspective. - **He’s not trying to learn.** If he’s not willing to respect your knowledge (e.g., not using the dishwasher on cast iron, not pre-buttering toast), then he’s not actually interested in cooking—just in using your tools. ### **What You Could Do Next:** - **Locking it up is a valid (if extreme) move.** If he’s still refusing to change, this forces him to either: - **Respect your boundaries** (and learn proper kitchen habits), or - **Admit he doesn’t care enough to fix his behavior** (which would be a problem for the relationship). - **Consider a compromise:** Maybe he can cook in a separate space (like a portable stove) while you teach him the right way to use your tools. - **Have a serious talk about respect.** If he can’t respect your things, he may struggle with respecting other boundaries in the relationship. ### **Final Verdict:** You’re **not** the one in the wrong here. His behavior is unreasonable, and your frustration is justified. If he can’t meet you halfway, that’s on him—not you. Would you like help drafting a way to communicate this to him in a way that’s firm but fair? Or are you leaning toward enforcing the "ban" as a last resort?
